title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 851–854 (Night 193, continuing nights-192), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 193 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. The stewardess begs the Lady Budūr to stop a jest that could cost them their lives if it reached her father; Budūr insists a handsome youth spent the night with her, and when the old woman denies it she looks at her hand, finds Qamar al-Zamān’s ring on her finger in place of her own, and in her fury cuts the stewardess down with a sword. The household runs to King al-Ghayūr; Budūr asks him where the young man is who slept beside her, tears her clothes and stares wildly about her, and he has her bound with an iron chain about her neck to a window of the palace. Grief-stricken, the king proclaims that whoever cures her shall marry her and have half the kingdom, and whoever fails shall lose his head; forty physicians are beheaded and forty astrologers crucified before everyone holds back. Budūr, wasting with love, recites two short poems, and so three years pass. Then her foster brother Marzawān, who loves her more than a brother, returns from distant travels. His mother tells the eunuch at the door that her daughter, brought up with Budūr, longs to visit her, and the next night she brings Marzawān in disguised in women’s clothes. He reads conjurations from his books, but Budūr knows him at once, speaks to him sensibly, denies that she is mad and recites three lines on love as a madness sweeter than sanity. Marzawān sees that she is in love and asks her to tell him her story, in the hope that he can deliver her, and dawn overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الثَّالِثَةُ وَالتِّسْعُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-thālithatu wa-al-tisʿūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the third and the ninety after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and ninety-third night,
sentences.n: al-thālitha, “the third”, feminine to agree with layla; then wa-al-tisʿūna, “and the ninety”, and baʿda al-miʾa, “after the hundred”, as in the nights before. The ئ of المائة is printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ الْقَهْرَمَانَةَ قَالَتْ لِلسَّيِّدَةِ بُدُورَ بِاللَّهِ عَلَيْكِ يَاسَيِّدَتِي لَاتَمْزَحِي هٰذَا الْمِزَاحَ الْخَارِجَ عَنِ الْحَدِّ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-qahramānata qālat li-al-sayyidati Budūra bi-Allāhi ʿalayki yā sayyidatī lā tamzaḥī hādhā al-mizāḥa al-khārija ʿani al-ḥaddi
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that the-stewardess said to-the-lady Budūr: By-God upon-you, O-my-lady, do-not jest this the-jesting the-going-out from the-limit,
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the stewardess said to the Lady Budūr, “I beg you by God, my lady, do not carry this jest so far beyond the bounds,
sentences.n: The night takes up the stewardess’s plea where the last broke off, repeating it almost word for word. bi-Allāhi ʿalayki, “by God (I lay it) upon you”, a set form of entreaty: bi- is the bi- of adjuring, and ʿalayki is feminine, addressed to Budūr. The print runs yā into sayyidatī, ياسيدتي, and lā into its verb, لاتمزحي; the spacing is kept. lā tamzaḥī, feminine prohibition; mazaḥa takes its own noun, mizāḥ, as object. al-khārij ʿan al-ḥadd, “going out beyond the limit”. li-, “to”, marks the one addressed. Budūr takes no tanwīn, as a woman’s name.

sentences.t: فَإِنَّهُ رُبَّمَا يَبْلُغُ أَبَاكِ هٰذَا الْمِزَاحُ فَمَنْ يُخَلِّصُنَا مِنْ يَدِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-innahu rubbamā yablughu abāki hādhā al-mizāḥu fa-man yukhalliṣunā min yadihi
sentences.l: For-indeed-it (is that) perhaps reaches your-father this the-jesting; then-who saves-us from his-hand?
sentences.i: for this jest may reach your father, and then who will save us from his hand?”
sentences.n: fa-innahu, “for it is (so) that”: -hu here is the pronoun of the matter, pointing to the whole clause that follows. rubbamā, “perhaps”; its shadda is printed. balagha takes the person reached as its direct object, abāki, “your father”. khallaṣa min, Form II, “to rescue from”. At the end of Night 192 the same question ran fa-man kāna yukhalliṣunā; here it is plainer.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهَا الْمَلِكَةُ بُدُورُ إِنَّهُ كَانَ غُلَامٌ بَائِتًا عِنْدِي فِي هٰذِهِ اللَّيْلَةِ وَهُوَ مِنْ أَحْسَنِ النَّاسِ وَجْهًا
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahā al-malikatu Budūru innahu kāna ghulāmun bāʾitan ʿindī fī hādhihi al-laylati wa-huwa min aḥsani al-nāsi wajhan
sentences.l: And-said to-her the-queen Budūr: Indeed-it (is that) was a-lad spending-the-night with-me in this the-night, and-he (is) of (the) fairest (of) the-people (in) face.
sentences.i: Queen Budūr said to her, “A young man spent this night with me, and he is one of the fairest of men in face.”
sentences.n: innahu kāna ghulāmun bāʾitan, “it is so that a lad was spending the night”: ghulām is printed without the alif of the accusative, so it is the subject of kāna, nominative, and bāʾitan, “spending the night” (active participle of bāta), its predicate. The order, with an indefinite subject standing first, is loose but readable. The ئ of بائتا is printed. wajhan, accusative of specification, “in respect of face”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهَا الْقَهْرَمَانَةُ سَلَامَةُ عَقْلِكِ مَا كَانَ أَحَدٌ بَائِتًا عِنْدَكِ فِي هٰذِهِ اللَّيْلَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahā al-qahramānatu salāmatu ʿaqliki mā kāna aḥadun bāʾitan ʿindaki fī hādhihi al-laylati
sentences.l: And-said to-her the-stewardess: (The) soundness (of) your-mind! Not was anyone spending-the-night with-you in this the-night.
sentences.i: The stewardess said to her, “God keep your wits! No one spent this night with you.”
sentences.n: salāmatu ʿaqliki, “the soundness of your mind”, an exclamation with the wish left unsaid, “(may God keep) your mind sound”; said, as here, to someone who seems to be talking nonsense. mā kāna aḥadun …, “there was not anyone …”.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذٰلِكَ نَظَرَتْ بُدُورُ إِلَى يَدِهَا فَوَجَدَتْ خَاتَمَ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ فِي إِصْبَعِهَا وَلَمْ تَجِدْ خَاتَمَهَا
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika naẓarat Budūru ilā yadihā fa-wajadat khātama Qamari al-Zamāni fī iṣbaʿihā wa-lam tajid khātamahā
sentences.l: So-at that, looked Budūr at her-hand, and-she-found (the) ring (of) Qamar al-Zamān on her-finger, and-not she-found her-ring.
sentences.i: At that Budūr looked at her hand, and found Qamar al-Zamān’s ring on her finger and her own ring gone.
sentences.n: fa-ʿinda dhālika, “and at that”, the text’s usual hinge. In the night, while the jinn watched, Qamar al-Zamān had taken her ring and put his own on her finger as she slept; this is the proof that he was real. lam tajid, jussive of wajada, “to find”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لِلْقَهْرَمَانَةِ وَيْلَكِ يَا مَلْعُونَةُ يَا خَائِنَةُ أَتَكْذِبِينَ عَلَيَّ وَتَقُولِينَ مَا كَانَ أَحَدٌ بَائِتًا عِنْدِي وَتَحْلِفِينَ لِي بِاللَّهِ بَاطِلًا
sentences.tr: fa-qālat li-al-qahramānati waylaki yā malʿūnatu yā khāʾinatu a-takdhibīna ʿalayya wa-taqūlīna mā kāna aḥadun bāʾitan ʿindī wa-taḥlifīna lī bi-Allāhi bāṭilan
sentences.l: And-she-said to-the-stewardess: Woe-to-you, O cursed-one, O treacherous-one! Do-you-lie against-me and-say: Not was anyone spending-the-night with-me, and-swear to-me by-God falsely?
sentences.i: She said to the stewardess, “Woe to you, you cursed, treacherous woman! Will you lie to my face, and tell me that no one spent the night with me, and swear to me falsely by God?”
sentences.n: waylaki, “woe to you”, accusative, with the feminine suffix. a-, the question prefix. kadhaba ʿalā, “to lie against, lie to”. ḥalafa li- … bi-, “to swear to (someone) by”: li- marks the one sworn to, bi- what one swears by. bāṭilan, “falsely”, an adverbial accusative. The shadda of عليّ and the ئ of خائنة are printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتِ الْقَهْرَمَانَةُ وَاللَّهِ مَاكَذَبْتُ عَلَيْكِ وَلَا حَلَفْتُ بَاطِلًا
sentences.tr: fa-qālati al-qahramānatu wa-Allāhi mā kadhabtu ʿalayki wa-lā ḥalaftu bāṭilan
sentences.l: And-said the-stewardess: By-God, not I-lied against-you, and-not I-swore falsely.
sentences.i: The stewardess said, “By God, I have not lied to you, nor sworn falsely.”
sentences.n: wa-Allāhi, “by God”: wa- here is the wāw of oaths, not “and”. The print runs mā into its verb, ماكذبت; the spacing is kept.

sentences.t: فَاغْتَاظَتْ مِنْهَا السِّتُّ بُدُورُ وَسَحَبَتْ سَيْفًا كَانَ عِنْدَهَا وَضَرَبَتْ بِهِ الْقَهْرَمَانَةَ فَقَتَلَهَا
sentences.tr: fa-ightāẓat minhā al-sittu Budūru wa-saḥabat sayfan kāna ʿindahā wa-ḍarabat bihi al-qahramānata fa-qatalahā
sentences.l: So-became-enraged at-her the-Lady Budūr, and-drew a-sword (that) was with-her, and-struck with-it the-stewardess, and-it-killed-her.
sentences.i: The Lady Budūr flew into a rage with her, drew a sword she kept by her, and struck the stewardess with it, and it killed her.
sentences.n: ightāẓa min, Form VIII, “to be enraged at”. al-sitt, “the lady”, a title used with the names of noblewomen, as with al-Sitt Budūr from here on. saḥaba, “to drag, draw out”. ḍaraba bi-, “to strike with”: bi- marks the weapon. fa-qatalahā is masculine, “and it (or he) killed her”: read as it stands, the subject is the sword, sayf (m.); the feminine fa-qatalathā, “and she killed her”, would be the expected wording, and the print may have dropped a ت, but the masculine is kept and read with the sword as subject.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذٰلِكَ صَاحَ الْخَادِمُ وَالْجَوَارِي وَالسَّرَارِي عَلَيْهَا وَرَاحُوا إِلَى أَبِيهَا وَأَعْلَمُوهُ بِحَالِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika ṣāḥa al-khādimu wa-al-jawārī wa-al-sarārī ʿalayhā wa-rāḥū ilā abīhā wa-aʿlamūhu bi-ḥālihā
sentences.l: So-at that, cried-out the-eunuch and-the-slave-girls and-the-concubines over-her, and-they-went to her-father and-informed-him of-her-state.
sentences.i: At that the eunuch, the slave girls and the concubines cried out over her, and went to her father and told him how it was with her.
sentences.n: al-khādim, “the servant”, in a palace usually the eunuch who keeps the women’s quarters. sarārī, plural of surriyya, “concubine”. ṣāḥa ʿalā, “to cry out at, over”. The verb ṣāḥa is singular before its several subjects, as a verb that comes first may be; rāḥū and aʿlamūhu then turn plural, masculine for the mixed company. aʿlama bi-, Form IV, “to inform of”: bi- marks the news given.

sentences.t: فَأَتَى الْمَلِكُ إِلَى ابْنَتِهِ السِّتِّ بُدُورَ مِنْ وَقْتِهِ وَسَاعَتِهِ وَقَالَ لَهَا يَا بِنْتِي مَا خَبَرُكِ فَقَالَتْ يَا أَبِي أَيْنَ الشَّابُّ الَّذِي كَانَ نَائِمًا بِجَانِبِي فِي هٰذِهِ اللَّيْلَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-atā al-maliku ilā ibnatihi al-sitti Budūra min waqtihi wa-sāʿatihi wa-qāla lahā yā bintī mā khabaruki fa-qālat yā abī ayna al-shābbu alladhī kāna nāʾiman bi-jānibī fī hādhihi al-laylati
sentences.l: So-came the-king to his-daughter the-Lady Budūr from his-time and-his-hour, and-said to-her: O my-daughter, what (is) your-news? And-she-said: O my-father, where (is) the-youth who was sleeping at-my-side in this the-night?
sentences.i: The king came to his daughter, the Lady Budūr, that very hour, and said to her, “My daughter, what has happened to you?” She said, “Father, where is the young man who was sleeping beside me tonight?”
sentences.n: min waqtihi wa-sāʿatihi, “from his time and his hour”, at once, a set phrase. atā ilā, “to come to”. mā khabaruki, “what is your news”, that is, what is the matter with you. bi-jānibī, “at my side”: bi- of place, “at, beside”. The ئ of نائما is printed.

sentences.t: وَطَارَ عَقْلُهَا مِنْ دِمَاغِهَا وَصَارَتْ تَلْتَفِتُ بِعَيْنِهَا يَمِينًا وَشِمَالًا ثُمَّ شَقَّتْ ثَوْبَهَا إِلَى ذَيْلِهَا
sentences.tr: wa-ṭāra ʿaqluhā min dimāghihā wa-ṣārat taltafitu bi-ʿaynihā yamīnan wa-shimālan thumma shaqqat thawbahā ilā dhaylihā
sentences.l: And-flew her-reason from her-brain, and-she-began to-turn with-her-eye right and-left; then she-tore her-garment to its-hem.
sentences.i: Her wits flew from her head, and she kept casting her eyes to right and left; then she tore her gown down to the hem.
sentences.n: ṭāra ʿaqluhu, “his reason flew”, the text’s stock phrase for going out of one’s mind. ṣāra with an imperfect, “to begin, take to (doing)”. iltafata, Form VIII, “to turn and look”; bi-ʿaynihā, “with her eye”: bi- marks the means. To tear one’s garment is a sign of frantic grief.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَى أَبُوهَا تِلْكَ الْفِعَالَ أَمَرَ الْجَوَارِيَ أَنْ يُمْسِكُوهَا فَمَسَكُوهَا وَقَيَّدُوهَا وَجَعَلُوا فِي رَقَبَتِهَا سِلْسِلَةً مِنْ حَدِيدٍ وَرَبَطُوهَا فِى الشُّبَّاكِ الَّذِي فِى الْقَصْرِ وَتَرَكُوهَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾā abūhā tilka al-fiʿāla amara al-jawāriya an yumsikūhā fa-masakūhā wa-qayyadūhā wa-jaʿalū fī raqabatihā silsilatan min ḥadīdin wa-rabaṭūhā fī al-shubbāki alladhī fī al-qaṣri wa-tarakūhā
sentences.l: And-when saw her-father those the-deeds, he-ordered the-slave-girls that they-seize-her; so-they-seized-her and-fettered-her, and-put on her-neck a-chain of iron, and-tied-her to the-window that (is) in the-palace, and-left-her.
sentences.i: When her father saw her do these things, he ordered the slave girls to hold her; so they held her and bound her, put an iron chain on her neck, tied her to the window of the palace and left her there.
sentences.n: fiʿāl, “deeds, doings”, a plural of fiʿl. The slave girls are women, but the verbs that follow are masculine plural, yumsikūhā, masakūhā, qayyadūhā …, where Classical Arabic wants the feminine (yumsiknahā …): the masculine plural standing for both genders is a common Middle Arabic habit. amsaka, Form IV, “to seize”, then masaka, Form I, in the same sense, a colloquial form. The print writes fī with ى twice in this line, فى; it is kept. The shadda of قيّدوها is printed. The shubbāk is a barred window. A chain round the neck was the usual treatment of the mad.

sentences.t: هٰذَا مَا كَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِ الْمَلِكَةِ بُدُورَ وَأَمَّا مَاكَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِ أَبِيهَا الْمَلِكِ الْغَيُورِ فَإِنَّهُ لَمَّا رَأَى مَاجَرَى عَلَى ابْنَتِهِ السِّتِّ بُدُورَ ضَاقَتْ عَلَيْهِ الدُّنْيَا لِأَنَّهُ كَانَ يُحِبُّهَا وَمَاهَانَ عَلَيْهِ أَمْرُهَا
sentences.tr: hādhā mā kāna min amri al-malikati Budūra wa-ammā mā kāna min amri abīhā al-maliki al-Ghayūri fa-innahu lammā raʾā mā jarā ʿalā ibnatihi al-sitti Budūra ḍāqat ʿalayhi al-dunyā li-annahu kāna yuḥibbuhā wa-mā hāna ʿalayhi amruhā
sentences.l: This (is) what was of (the) affair (of) the-queen Budūr. And-as-for what was of (the) affair (of) her-father the-king al-Ghayūr, then-indeed-he, when he-saw what befell upon his-daughter the-Lady Budūr, grew-narrow upon-him the-world, because-he was loving-her, and-not was-light upon-him her-affair.
sentences.i: So much for Queen Budūr. As for her father, King al-Ghayūr: when he saw what had befallen his daughter, the Lady Budūr, the world grew narrow for him, for he loved her, and her plight weighed on him.
sentences.n: The storyteller’s formula for leaving one thread to take up another. wa-ammā … fa-, “as for …, then”. The print runs mā into the following word three times here, ماكان, ماجرى, وماهان; the spacing is kept. jarā ʿalā, “to happen to”. ḍāqat ʿalayhi al-dunyā, “the world became narrow upon him”, he was in anguish. li-anna, “because”: li-, “for”, giving the reason. hāna ʿalā, “to be light, of small account to”; mā hāna ʿalayhi amruhā, “her case was no light thing to him”. The shadda of يحبّها and the hamza of رأى are printed.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذٰلِكَ أَحْضَرَ الْحُكَمَاءَ وَالْمُنَجِّمِينَ وَأَصْحَابَ الْأَقْلَامِ وَقَالَ لَهُمْ كُلُّ مَنْ أَبْرَأَ بِنْتِي مِمَّاهِيَ فِيهِ زَوَّجْتُهُ بِهَا وَأَعْطَيْتُهُ نِصْفَ مَمْلَكَتِي
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika aḥḍara al-ḥukamāʾa wa-al-munajjimīna wa-aṣḥāba al-aqlāmi wa-qāla lahum kullu man abraʾa bintī mimmā hiya fīhi zawwajtuhu bihā wa-aʿṭaytuhu niṣfa mamlakatī
sentences.l: So-at that, he-summoned the-sages and-the-astrologers and-(the)-masters (of) the-pens, and-said to-them: Every-one who cures my-daughter from-what she (is) in-it, I-marry-him to-her and-I-give-him half (of) my-kingdom.
sentences.i: Then he summoned the physicians, the astrologers and the men of the pen, and said to them, “Whoever cures my daughter of what ails her, I will marry him to her and give him half my kingdom;
sentences.n: ḥakīm, plural ḥukamāʾ, “sage”, and also “physician”, which is the sense here. aṣḥāb al-aqlām, “masters of the pens”, the learned men who write charms and calculate. abraʾa, Form IV, “to heal, cure”; its hamza is printed. mimmā = min mā, “from what”; the print runs it into hiya, مماهي, and the spacing is kept. zawwaja … bi-, Form II, “to marry (him) to”: the verb takes bi- for the bride. The perfects zawwajtuhu and aʿṭaytuhu after a condition carry future sense, “I will marry … I will give”.

sentences.t: وَمَنْ تَقَدَّمَ إِلَيْهَا وَلَمْ يُبْرِئْهَا أَضْرِبْ عُنُقَهُ وَأُعَلِّقْ رَأْسَهُ عَلَى بَابِ قَصْرِهَا
sentences.tr: wa-man taqaddama ilayhā wa-lam yubriʾhā aḍrib ʿunuqahu wa-uʿalliq raʾsahu ʿalā bābi qaṣrihā
sentences.l: And-whoever comes-forward to-her and-not cures-her, I-strike his-neck and-I-hang his-head upon (the) gate (of) her-palace.
sentences.i: but whoever comes to her and does not cure her, I will strike off his head and hang it over the gate of her palace.”
sentences.n: man, “whoever”, here a condition: the answering verbs are given the jussive, aḍrib, uʿalliq, as Classical grammar wants; the print shows no mood either way. ḍaraba ʿunuqahu, “to strike his neck”, to behead. The ئ of يبرئها and the hamza of رأسه are printed.

sentences.t: فَصَارَ كُلُّ مَنْ دَخَلَ عَلَيْهَا وَلَمْ يُبْرِئْهَا يُضْرَبُ عُنُقُهُ وَيُعَلَّقُ رَأْسُهُ عَلَى بَابِ الْقَصْرِ إِلَى أَنْ قَطَعَ مِنْ أَجْلِهَا أَرْبَعِينَ رَأْسَ رَجُلٍ مِنَ الْحُكَمَاءِ وَصَلَبَ أَرْبَعِينَ رَجُلًا مِنَ الْمُنَجِّمِينَ
sentences.tr: fa-ṣāra kullu man dakhala ʿalayhā wa-lam yubriʾhā yuḍrabu ʿunuquhu wa-yuʿallaqu raʾsuhu ʿalā bābi al-qaṣri ilā an qaṭaʿa min ajlihā arbaʿīna raʾsa rajulin mina al-ḥukamāʾi wa-ṣalaba arbaʿīna rajulan mina al-munajjimīna
sentences.l: And-came every-one who entered upon-her and-not cured-her (to) be-struck his-neck and-be-hung his-head upon (the) gate (of) the-palace, until that he-cut-off for her-sake forty head(s) (of) man of the-sages, and-crucified forty men of the-astrologers.
sentences.i: So everyone who went in to her and did not cure her had his head struck off and hung over the palace gate, until for her sake he had cut off the heads of forty of the physicians and crucified forty of the astrologers.
sentences.n: ṣāra with an imperfect again, of what now happened each time; yuḍrabu and yuʿallaqu are passive. arbaʿīna raʾsa rajulin, “forty head of man”: a number from eleven to ninety-nine takes its counted noun in the singular accusative. The print spells raʾs here as راس, without the hamza it printed in رأسه just before, and the reading supplies it. min ajlihā, “for her sake”. ṣalaba, “to crucify”, also “to hang up, gibbet”. The shadda of المنجّمين is printed.

sentences.t: فَتَوَقَّفَتْ جَمِيعُ النَّاسِ عَنْهَا وَعَجَزَتْ جَمِيعُ الْحُكَمَاءِ عَنْ دَوَائِهَا وَأَشْكَلَتْ حِكَايَتُهَا عَلَى أَهْلِ الْعُلُومِ وَأَرْبَابِ الْأَقْلَامِ
sentences.tr: fa-tawaqqafat jamīʿu al-nāsi ʿanhā wa-ʿajazat jamīʿu al-ḥukamāʾi ʿan dawāʾihā wa-ashkalat ḥikāyatuhā ʿalā ahli al-ʿulūmi wa-arbābi al-aqlāmi
sentences.l: So-held-back all the-people from-her, and-fell-short all the-sages from her-cure, and-was-obscure her-case upon (the) people (of) the-sciences and-(the)-lords (of) the-pens.
sentences.i: Then everyone held back from her; all the physicians were powerless to cure her, and her case baffled the men of learning and the masters of the pen.
sentences.n: tawaqqafa ʿan, Form V, “to hold back from”. The verbs are feminine with jamīʿ, “all”, agreeing in sense with the plural that follows. ʿajaza ʿan, “to be unable to”. ashkala ʿalā, Form IV, “to be obscure to, puzzle”. ḥikāya, “story”, here “her case”. The ئ of دوائها is printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ السِّتَّ بُدُورَ لَمَّا زَادَ بِهَا الْوَجْدُ وَالْغَرَامُ وَأَضَرَّبِهَا الْعِشْقُ وَالْهُيَامُ أَجْرَتِ الْعَبَرَاتِ وَأَنْشَدَتْ هٰذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-sitta Budūra lammā zāda bihā al-wajdu wa-al-gharāmu wa-aḍarra bihā al-ʿishqu wa-al-huyāmu ajrati al-ʿabarāti wa-anshadat hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: Then indeed the-Lady Budūr, when increased in-her the-passion and-the-longing, and-harmed her the-love and-the-love-madness, she-made-flow the-tears and-recited these the-verses:
sentences.i: Then the Lady Budūr, as her passion and longing grew and love and its madness wore her down, let her tears flow and recited these verses:
sentences.n: Rhymed prose: al-wajdu wa-al-gharāmu, al-ʿishqu wa-al-huyāmu, two pairs of near-synonyms for love ending in -ām. zāda bi-, “to grow in (someone)”: bi- marks the one it grows in. aḍarra bi-, Form IV, “to harm”: the verb takes bi- for the one harmed. The print runs it into bihā, واضرّبها, with a shadda on the ر; the spacing and the mark are kept. huyām, love-madness, properly a raging thirst. ajrā, Form IV, “to make flow”; al-ʿabarāt, “the tears”.

sentences.t:
غَرَامِيْ فِيْكَ يَا قَمَرِيْ غَرِيْمِيْ * وَذِكْرُكَ فِيْ دُجَى لَيْلِيْ نَدِيْمِيْ
اَبِيْتُ وَاَضْلُعِيْ فِيْهَا لَهِيْبُ * يُحَاكِيْ حَرُّهُ نَارَ الْجَحِيْمِ
بُلِيْتُ بِفَرْطِ وَجْدٍ وَاحْتِرَاقٍ * عَذَابِيْ مِنْهُمَا اَضْحَى اَلِيْمِيْ
sentences.tr:
gharāmī fīka yā qamarī gharīmī * wa-dhikruka fī dujā laylī nadīmī
abītu wa-aḍluʿī fīhā lahību * yuḥākī ḥarruhu nāra al-jaḥīmi
bulītu bi-farṭi wajdin wa-iḥtirāqin * ʿadhābī minhumā aḍḥā alīmī
sentences.l:
My-passion for-you, O my-moon, (is) my-creditor, * and-remembering-you in (the) darkness (of) my-night (is) my-boon-companion.
I-pass-the-night, and-my-ribs in-them (is) a-flame * resembles its-heat (the) fire (of) the-Hell.
I-am-afflicted with-excess (of) passion and-burning; * my-torment from-the-two has-become my-anguish.
sentences.i:
My passion for you, my moon, dogs me like a creditor, * and the thought of you is my companion in the dark of my night.
I lie through the night with a flame among my ribs * whose heat is like the fire of Hell.
I am stricken with passion beyond measure and with burning, * and the torment of the two has become my anguish.
sentences.n: The print points the verse, and its pointing is kept; as often it sets a sukūn on long ī (فِيْكَ, قَمَرِيْ) and writes the hamza of اَبِيْتُ, وَاَضْلُعِيْ, اَضْحَى, اَلِيْمِيْ as a vowel on bare alif. “My moon” glances at the beloved’s name, Qamar al-Zamān. gharāmī … gharīmī play on one root: gharām is consuming love, and gharīm the creditor who clings to his debtor and will not let him go. nadīm, the companion at wine and talk through the night. lahību is printed without tanwīn, where lahībun is expected. ḥākā, Form III, “to resemble”. bulītu, passive, “I have been afflicted”; bi- marks the affliction. alīmī, “my painful one”: alīm is “painful”, and the -ī is forced by the rhyme on -īmī; the sense is “my torment has become my pain”, or, taking the suffix loosely, “has become painful to me”. The line is somewhat strained, and the translation follows the likelier sense.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهَا تَأَوَّهَتْ وَأَنْشَدَتْ أَيْضًا تَقُولُ
sentences.tr: thumma innahā taʾawwahat wa-anshadat ayḍan taqūlu
sentences.l: Then indeed-she groaned and-recited also, saying:
sentences.i: Then she sighed, and recited these lines too:
sentences.n: taʾawwaha, Form V, “to say āh, to sigh, groan”; the shadda of تاوّهت is printed, without the hamza, which the reading supplies. anshadat … taqūlu, “she recited, saying”, the imperfect standing as a circumstantial clause.

sentences.t:
سَلَامِي عَلَى الْاَحْبَابِ فِي كُلِّ مَنْزِلِ * فَاِنِّي اِلَى نَحْوِ الْحَبِيْبِ اُرِيْدُ
سَلَامِي عَلَيْكُمْ لَا سَلَامَ مُوَدِّعٍ * سَلَامٌ كَثِيْرٌ لَا يَزَالُ يَزِيْدُ
وَاِنِّي لَاَهْوَاكُمْ وَاَهْوَى دِيَارَكُمْ * وَلٰكِنَّنِي عَمَّا اُرِيْدُ بَعِيْدُ
sentences.tr:
salāmī ʿalā al-aḥbābi fī kulli manzili * fa-innī ilā naḥwi al-ḥabībi urīdu
salāmī ʿalaykum lā salāma muwaddiʿin * salāmun kathīrun lā yazālu yazīdu
wa-innī la-ahwākum wa-ahwā diyārakum * wa-lākinnanī ʿammā urīdu baʿīdu
sentences.l:
My-greeting (be) upon the-loved-ones in every dwelling, * for-indeed-I to (the) direction (of) the-beloved want (to go).
My-greeting (be) upon-you, not (the) greeting (of) one-taking-leave, * a-greeting abundant (that) not ceases increasing.
And-indeed-I surely-love-you and-love your-dwellings, * but-I (am) from-what I-want far.
sentences.i:
My greeting to the loved ones in every place they dwell, * for it is toward the beloved that I long to go.
My greeting to you, and not the greeting of farewell, * but a greeting without stint that grows for ever.
I love you, and I love the places where you live, * and yet I am far from what I long for.
sentences.n: The print points the verse, and its pointing is kept; it writes the hamza of اِلَى, اِنِّي, اُرِيْدُ and the rest as a vowel on bare alif. manzili, “dwelling”, is printed with a bare kasra where manzilin is expected. ilā naḥwi, “toward”; urīdu, “I want”, with “to go” understood. lā salāma muwaddiʿin, “not the greeting of one who bids farewell”: her greeting is not a last one. lā yazālu yazīdu, “does not cease to increase”. la-ahwākum, la- of emphasis after inna, “I do love you”; hawā, “to love, desire”. ʿammā = ʿan mā, “from what”. The verses are addressed to the beloved in the plural, a common courtesy in love poetry.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا فَرَغَتِ السِّتُّ بُدُورُ مِنْ إِنْشَادِ هٰذِهِ الْأَشْعَارِ بَكَتْ حَتَّى مَرِضَتْ عَيْنَاهَا وَتَغَيَّرَتْ وَجَنَاتُهَا ثُمَّ إِنَّهَا اسْتَمَرَّتْ عَلَى هٰذَا الْحَالِ ثَلٰثَ سِنِينَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā faraghati al-sittu Budūru min inshādi hādhihi al-ashʿāri bakat ḥattā mariḍat ʿaynāhā wa-taghayyarat wajanātuhā thumma innahā istamarrat ʿalā hādhā al-ḥāli thalātha sinīna
sentences.l: And-when finished the-Lady Budūr from reciting these the-poems, she-wept until became-sick her-two-eyes and-changed her-cheeks. Then indeed-she continued upon this the-state three years.
sentences.i: When the Lady Budūr had finished reciting these verses, she wept until her eyes were sore and her cheeks lost their colour. And so she remained for three years.
sentences.n: faragha min, “to be done with”. inshād, verbal noun of anshada, “reciting”. ʿaynāhā, dual, “her two eyes”. wajanāt, plural of wajna, “cheek”, the plural used for a single face. istamarra ʿalā, Form X, “to continue in”. ḥāl may be masculine or feminine; here it takes the masculine hādhā, as often in the text. The print spells thalāth defectively with the dagger alif, ثلٰث, and the mark is kept. thalātha sinīna, accusative of time, “for three years”.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ لَهَا أَخٌ مِنَ الرَّضَاعِ يُسَمَّى مَرْزَوَانَ وَكَانَ سَافَرَ إِلَى أَقْصَي الْبِلَادِ وَغَابَ عَنْهَا تِلْكَ الْمُدَّةَ بِطُولِهَا وَكَانَ يُحِبُّهَا مَحَبَّةً زِيَادَةً عَلَى مَحَبَّةِ الْإِخْوَةِ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna lahā akhun mina al-raḍāʿi yusammā Marzawāna wa-kāna sāfara ilā aqṣā al-bilādi wa-ghāba ʿanhā tilka al-muddata bi-ṭūlihā wa-kāna yuḥibbuhā maḥabbatan ziyādatan ʿalā maḥabbati al-ikhwati
sentences.l: And-there-was to-her a-brother from the-suckling (who) was-named Marzawān, and-he-had travelled to (the) farthest (of) the-lands and-been-absent from-her that the-period in-its-length. And-he-was loving-her a-love (an) increase upon (the) love (of) the-brothers.
sentences.i: She had a foster brother named Marzawān, who had travelled to the farthest lands and been away from her the whole of that time. He loved her with a love beyond the love of brothers.
sentences.n: akh mina al-raḍāʿ, “a brother by suckling”, a foster brother, nursed at the same breast; Islamic law treats the tie as close kin. Marzawān, a Persian name, here given no tanwīn. yusammā, passive of sammā, “to name”, takes the name in the accusative. kāna sāfara, “he had travelled”, kāna with the perfect for the pluperfect. The print spells aqṣā, “farthest”, with a dotted ي, اقصي, where ى is usual. bi-ṭūlihā, “in its length”: bi- “with”, the whole of it. maḥabbatan, the verb’s own noun as object. ziyādatan, “an increase”, a noun standing as an adjective, “greater”, a colloquial turn; ziyāda ʿalā, “more than”. ikhwa, “brothers”, plural of akh. The shadda of يحبّها is printed.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا حَضَرَ دَخَلَ عَلَى وَالِدَتِهِ وَسَأَلَهَا عَنْ أُخْتِهِ السِّتِّ بُدُورَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā ḥaḍara dakhala ʿalā wālidatihi wa-saʾalahā ʿan ukhtihi al-sitti Budūra
sentences.l: And-when he-arrived, he-went-in upon his-mother and-asked-her about his-sister the-Lady Budūr.
sentences.i: When he came home, he went in to his mother and asked her about his sister, the Lady Budūr.
sentences.n: ḥaḍara, “to be present, arrive”. wālida, “mother”. The hamza of سألها is printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ يَا وَلَدِي إِنَّ أُخْتَكَ حَصَلَ لَهَا جُنُونٌ وَمَضَى لَهَا ثَلٰثُ سِنِينَ وَفِي رَقَبَتِهَا سِلْسِلَةٌ مِنْ حَدِيدٍ وَعَجَزَتْ جَمِيعُ أَهْلِ الطِّبِّ وَأَهْلِ الْحِكْمَةِ عَنْ دَوَائِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu yā waladī inna ukhtaka ḥaṣala lahā junūnun wa-maḍā lahā thalāthu sinīna wa-fī raqabatihā silsilatun min ḥadīdin wa-ʿajazat jamīʿu ahli al-ṭibbi wa-ahli al-ḥikmati ʿan dawāʾihā
sentences.l: And-she-said to-him: O my-son, indeed your-sister, has-happened to-her madness, and-have-passed for-her three years, and-on her-neck (is) a-chain of iron, and-have-fallen-short all (the) people (of) the-medicine and-(the)-people (of) the-wisdom from her-cure.
sentences.i: She said to him, “My son, your sister has gone mad, and it is three years now that she has worn an iron chain on her neck, and all the doctors and the learned have failed to cure her.”
sentences.n: The print has اخيك, a misprint for اختك, “your sister”, corrected here: the mother is speaking of Budūr, as the feminine lahā, “to her”, shows. inna ukhtaka is followed by a whole sentence about her, ḥaṣala lahā junūnun, “madness has befallen her”: “as for your sister, madness has come upon her”. ḥaṣala li-, colloquial, “to happen to”: li- marks the one it happens to. maḍā lahā thalāthu sinīna, “three years have passed for her”: the verb stands first and stays masculine. The print again spells thalāth with the dagger alif, ثلٰث. ahl al-ṭibb, “the people of medicine”, doctors; ahl al-ḥikma, “the people of wisdom”, sages.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ مَرْزَوَانُ هٰذَا الْكَلَامَ قَالَ لَابُدَّ مِنْ دُخُولِي عَلَيْهَا لَعَلِّي أَعْرِفُ مَا بِهَا وَأَقْدِرُ عَلَى دَوَائِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa Marzawānu hādhā al-kalāma qāla lā budda min dukhūlī ʿalayhā laʿallī aʿrifu mā bihā wa-aqdiru ʿalā dawāʾihā
sentences.l: And-when heard Marzawān this the-speech, he-said: No escape from my-going-in upon-her; perhaps-I know what (is) in-her and-am-able for her-cure.
sentences.i: When Marzawān heard this he said, “I must go in to her; perhaps I can find out what is wrong with her and be able to cure her.”
sentences.n: lā budda min, “there is no escape from”, “I must”; the print runs lā into budda, لابد, and the spacing is kept. dukhūl ʿalā, “going in to (someone)”. laʿallī, “perhaps I”, laʿalla with the suffix -ī. mā bihā, “what is in her”, what ails her: bi- “in”. qadara ʿalā, “to be able to”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَتْ أُمُّهُ كَلَامَهُ قَالَتْ لَابُدَّ مِنْ دُخُولِكَ عَلَيْهَا وَلٰكِنْ تَمَهَّلْ إِلَى غَدٍ حَتَّى أَتَحَيَّلَ فِي أَمْرِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿat ummuhu kalāmahu qālat lā budda min dukhūlika ʿalayhā wa-lākin tamahhal ilā ghadin ḥattā ataḥayyala fī amrika
sentences.l: And-when heard his-mother his-speech, she-said: No escape from your-going-in upon-her, but wait till tomorrow, so-that I-contrive in your-affair.
sentences.i: When his mother heard what he said, she answered, “You shall certainly go in to her; but wait until tomorrow, so that I can find a way to manage it for you.”
sentences.n: tamahhal, Form V imperative, “take your time, wait”. ḥattā with the subjunctive, ataḥayyala, “so that I may contrive”; taḥayyala, Form V, from ḥīla, “stratagem”. The shaddas of تمهّل and اتحيّل are printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ أُمَّهُ تَرَجَّلَتْ إِلَى قَصْرِ السِّتِّ بُدُورَ وَاجْتَمَعَتْ بِالْخَادِمِ الْمُوَكَّلِ بِالْبَابِ وَأَهْدَتْ لَهُ هَدِيَّةً
sentences.tr: thumma inna ummahu tarajjalat ilā qaṣri al-sitti Budūra wa-ijtamaʿat bi-al-khādimi al-muwakkali bi-al-bābi wa-ahdat lahu hadiyyatan
sentences.l: Then indeed his-mother went-on-foot to (the) palace (of) the-Lady Budūr, and-met with-the-eunuch the-one-put-in-charge of-the-door, and-gave to-him a-gift.
sentences.i: Then his mother went on foot to the Lady Budūr’s palace, sought out the eunuch who kept the door, and gave him a present.
sentences.n: tarajjala, Form V, “to dismount, go on foot”, from rijl, “foot”: she went to the palace on foot. ijtamaʿa bi-, Form VIII, “to meet with”: bi- marks the one met. muwakkal bi-, Form II passive participle, “put in charge of”: bi- marks the charge. ahdā li-, Form IV, “to give as a gift to”. The shaddas of ترجّلت and الموكّل are printed.

sentences.t: وَقَالَتْ لَهُ إِنَّ لِي بِنْتًا وَقَدْ تَرَبَّتْ مَعَ السِّتِّ بُدُورَ وَقَدْ زَوَّجْتُهَا
sentences.tr: wa-qālat lahu inna lī bintan wa-qad tarabbat maʿa al-sitti Budūra wa-qad zawwajtuhā
sentences.l: And-she-said to-him: Indeed to-me (is) a-daughter, and-indeed she-was-brought-up with the-Lady Budūr, and-indeed I-have-married-her (off).
sentences.i: She said to him, “I have a daughter who was brought up with the Lady Budūr, and I have married her off;
sentences.n: The print has بذور, a misprint for بدور, corrected here. inna lī bintan, “I have a daughter”, literally “there is to me a daughter”: li- of possession. tarabbā, Form V, “to be brought up”. The mother’s story is a ruse: the “daughter” will be Marzawān in women’s clothes.

sentences.t: وَلَمَّاجَرَى لِسَيِّدَتِكَ مَا جَرَى صَارَ خَاطِرُهَا مُتَعَلِّقًا بِهَا وَأَنَا أَقْصِدُ مِنْ فَضْلِكَ فِي أَنَّ بِنْتِي تَأْتِي عِنْدَهَا سَاعَةً لِتَنْظُرَهَا ثُمَّ تَرْجِعَ مِنْ حَيْثُ جَاءَتْ وَلَايَعْلَمُ بِهَا أَحَدٌ
sentences.tr: wa-lammā jarā li-sayyidatika mā jarā ṣāra khāṭiruhā mutaʿalliqan bihā wa-anā aqṣidu min faḍlika fī anna bintī taʾtī ʿindahā sāʿatan li-tanẓurahā thumma tarjiʿa min ḥaythu jāʾat wa-lā yaʿlamu bihā aḥadun
sentences.l: and-when happened to-your-mistress what happened, became her-mind hanging on-her; and-I seek from your-kindness in that my-daughter comes to-her (for) an-hour to-see-her, then returns from where she-came, and-not knows of-her anyone.
sentences.i: and since what has happened to your mistress happened, her heart has been set on her. So I ask of your kindness that my daughter may come to her for an hour to see her and then go back the way she came, with no one knowing of it.”
sentences.n: The print runs lammā into jarā, ولماجرى; the spacing is kept. jarā li-, “to happen to”: li- marks the one it happens to; mā jarā, “what happened”, a deliberately vague phrase for her madness. khāṭir, “mind, heart”; mutaʿalliqan bi-, Form V participle, “attached to”: bi- marks what the heart clings to. qaṣada min faḍlika, “to ask of your kindness”, a polite formula; fī anna, “that”, a colloquial construction. li-tanẓurahā, li- of purpose with the subjunctive, “so that she may see her”; thumma tarjiʿa goes on in the subjunctive. wa-lā yaʿlamu bihā aḥadun, “with nobody knowing of her”, again run together in the print, ولايعلم. ʿalima bi-, “to know of”. The hamza of تأتي and جاءت is printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْخَادِمُ لَايُمْكِنُ ذٰلِكَ إِلَّا فِي اللَّيْلِ فَبَعْدَأَنْ يَأْتِيَ السُّلْطَانُ يَنْظُرُ ابْنَتَهُ وَيَخْرُجَ فَادْخُلِي أَنْتِ وَابْنَتُكِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-khādimu lā yumkinu dhālika illā fī al-layli fa-baʿda an yaʾtiya al-sulṭānu yanẓuru ibnatahu wa-yakhruja fa-udkhulī anti wa-ibnatuki
sentences.l: And-said the-eunuch: Not is-possible that except in the-night; so-after that comes the-sultan, looking-at his-daughter, and-goes-out, then-enter you and-your-daughter.
sentences.i: The eunuch said, “That cannot be, except at night: when the sultan has come to see his daughter and gone out again, then come in, you and your daughter.”
sentences.n: The print runs lā into yumkinu, لايمكن, and baʿda into an, فبعدان; the spacing is kept. baʿda an, “after”, with the subjunctive, yaʾtiya … wa-yakhruja. yanẓuru ibnatahu, “looking at his daughter”, an imperfect of purpose, “to see his daughter”. The king is called al-sulṭān here, as often in the tales. udkhulī anti wa-ibnatuki, “enter, you and your daughter”: the separate pronoun anti is expressed so that a second subject, ibnatuki, can be joined to the “you” already contained in the verb. The hamza of يأتي is printed.

sentences.t: فَقَبَّلَتِ الْعَجُوزُ يَدَ الْخَادِمِ وَخَرَجَتْ إِلَى بَيْتِهَا فَصَبَرَتْ إِلَى ثَانِي يَوْمٍ الْعِشَاءَ
sentences.tr: fa-qabbalati al-ʿajūzu yada al-khādimi wa-kharajat ilā baytihā fa-ṣabarat ilā thānī yawmin al-ʿishāʾa
sentences.l: So-kissed the-old-woman (the) hand (of) the-eunuch and-went-out to her-house, and-she-waited until (the) second day, the-nightfall.
sentences.i: The old woman kissed the eunuch’s hand and went home, and waited until nightfall on the following day.
sentences.n: qabbala, Form II, “to kiss”; its shadda is printed. thānī yawmin, “the second of days”, the next day, a colloquial phrase. al-ʿishāʾa, accusative of time, “at nightfall”, the hour of the evening prayer: “till the next day, at nightfall”. The phrase is loosely built and the reading is uncertain; it might also be meant as a single construct, ilā thānī yawmi al-ʿishāʾi.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا جَاءَ وَقْتُهُ قَامَتْ مِنْ وَقْتِهَا وَسَاعَتِهَا وَأَخَذَتْ وَلَدَهَا مَرْزَوَانَ وَأَلْبَسَتْهُ بَدْلَةً مِنْ ثِيَابِ النِّسَاءِ وَجَعَلَتْ يَدَهُ فِي يَدِهَا وَأَدْخَلَتْهُ الْقَصْرَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā jāʾa waqtuhu qāmat min waqtihā wa-sāʿatihā wa-akhadhat waladahā Marzawāna wa-albasathu badlatan min thiyābi al-nisāʾi wa-jaʿalat yadahu fī yadihā wa-adkhalathu al-qaṣra
sentences.l: And-when came its-time, she-rose from her-time and-her-hour, and-took her-son Marzawān, and-clothed-him (in) a-suit of (the) clothes (of) the-women, and-put his-hand in her-hand, and-brought-him-in (to) the-palace.
sentences.i: When the time came she rose that very hour, took her son Marzawān, dressed him in a suit of women’s clothes, put his hand in hers and led him into the palace.
sentences.n: waqtuhu, “its time”, the time of the evening. min waqtihā wa-sāʿatihā, “at once”, as before. albasa, Form IV, “to clothe”, takes two objects, the person and the clothes. badla, “suit of clothes”, a colloquial word. adkhala, Form IV, “to bring in”, here with the place as direct object.

sentences.t: وَلَا زَالَتْ تَمْشِي بِهِ حَتَّى أَوْصَلَتْهُ إِلَى الْخَادِمِ بَعْدَ انْصِرَافِ السُّلْطَانِ مِنْ عِنْدِ بِنْتِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-lā zālat tamshī bihi ḥattā awṣalathu ilā al-khādimi baʿda inṣirāfi al-sulṭāni min ʿindi bintihi
sentences.l: And-not she-ceased walking with-him until she-brought-him to the-eunuch, after (the) departure (of) the-sultan from with his-daughter.
sentences.i: She walked on with him until she had brought him to the eunuch, after the sultan had left his daughter.
sentences.n: lā zālat, “she did not cease”, so “she went on”; lā with the perfect in this phrase. mashā bi-, “to walk with, lead”: bi- marks the one taken along. awṣala, Form IV, “to bring to”. bintihi, “his daughter”; bint and ibna are both good Classical forms of the word, and the text uses both: the eunuch said ابنته above.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَآهَا الْخَادِمُ قَامَ وَاقِفًا وَقَالَ لَهَا ادْخُلِي وَلَا تُطِيلِى الْقُعُودَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾāhā al-khādimu qāma wāqifan wa-qāla lahā udkhulī wa-lā tuṭīlī al-quʿūda
sentences.l: And-when saw-her the-eunuch, he-rose standing and-said to-her: Enter, and-not make-long the-sitting.
sentences.i: When the eunuch saw her he got to his feet and said to her, “Go in, and do not stay long.”
sentences.n: The print has وانفا, a misprint for واقفا, corrected here. qāma wāqifan, “he rose standing”, got to his feet, a common pleonasm. lā tuṭīlī, feminine prohibition of aṭāla, Form IV, “to make long”; the print ends it with ى, تطيلى, and it is kept. The madda of رآها is printed.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا دَخَلَتِ الْعَجُوزُ بِوَلَدِهَا رَأَى مَرْزَوَانُ السِّتَّ بُدُورَ فِي تِلْكَ الْحَالَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā dakhalati al-ʿajūzu bi-waladihā raʾā Marzawānu al-sitta Budūra fī tilka al-ḥālati
sentences.l: And-when entered the-old-woman with-her-son, saw Marzawān the-Lady Budūr in that the-state.
sentences.i: When the old woman went in with her son, Marzawān saw the Lady Budūr in that sad state.
sentences.n: dakhala bi-, “to go in with, bring in”: bi- marks the one brought. raʾā is printed here without its hamza, راى, which the reading supplies.

sentences.t: فَسَلَّمَ عَلَيْهَا بَعْدَ أَنْ كَشَفَتْ عَنْهُ أُمُّهُ ثِيَابَ النِّسَاءِ فَأَخْرَجَ مَرْزَوَانُ الْكُتُبَ الَّتِي مَعَهُ وَأَوْقَدَ شَمْعَتَهُ وَقَرَأَ بَعْضَ أَقْسَامٍ
sentences.tr: fa-sallama ʿalayhā baʿda an kashafat ʿanhu ummuhu thiyāba al-nisāʾi fa-akhraja Marzawānu al-kutuba allatī maʿahu wa-awqada shamʿatahu wa-qaraʾa baʿḍa aqsāmin
sentences.l: So-he-greeted her after that uncovered from-him his-mother (the) clothes (of) the-women. Then-brought-out Marzawān the-books that (were) with-him, and-lit his-candle, and-read some (of) conjurations.
sentences.i: He greeted her, once his mother had taken the women’s clothes off him. Marzawān took out the books he had brought, lit his candle and read out some conjurations.
sentences.n: sallama ʿalā, Form II, “to greet”. kashafa ʿan, “to uncover, strip from”. Marzawān comes as a healer of the old school, with books of spells. aqsām is read here as the plural of qasam, “oath”: the adjurations recited over the possessed to drive out a jinn. The same letters are also the plural of qism, “part, section”, and “read some sections (of his books)” is possible; the doubt is left open. baʿḍa aqsāmin, with the second noun indefinite, is a loose colloquial turn. awqada, Form IV, “to kindle”. The hamza of قرأ is printed.

sentences.t: فَنَظَرَتْ إِلَيْهِ السِّتُّ بُدُورُ فَعَرَفَتْهُ وَقَالَتْ لَهُ يَا أَخِي أَنْتَ كُنْتَ سَافَرْتَ وَانْقَطَعَتْ أَخْبَارُكَ عَنَّا
sentences.tr: fa-naẓarat ilayhi al-sittu Budūru fa-ʿarafathu wa-qālat lahu yā akhī anta kunta sāfarta wa-inqaṭaʿat akhbāruka ʿannā
sentences.l: And-looked at-him the-Lady Budūr, and-she-knew-him, and-said to-him: O my-brother, you, you-had travelled, and-were-cut-off your-news from-us.
sentences.i: The Lady Budūr looked at him and knew him, and said to him, “My brother, you had gone on your travels, and we heard nothing more of you.”
sentences.n: She is lucid at once, which is the point: she is not mad. kunta sāfarta, “you had travelled”, kāna with the perfect for the pluperfect; anta set before it for emphasis. inqaṭaʿa, Form VII, “to be cut off”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا صَحِيحٌ وَلٰكِنْ رَدَّنِي اللَّهُ بِالسَّلَامَةِ وَأَرَدْتُ السَّفَرَ ثَانِيًا فَمَا رَدَّنِي عَنْهُ إِلَّا هٰذَا الْخَبَرُ الَّذِي سَمِعْتُهُ عَنْكِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā ṣaḥīḥun wa-lākin raddanī Allāhu bi-al-salāmati wa-aradtu al-safara thāniyan fa-mā raddanī ʿanhu illā hādhā al-khabaru alladhī samiʿtuhu ʿanki
sentences.l: And-he-said to-her: True; but returned-me God with-the-safety, and-I-wanted the-travelling a-second-time, and-not turned-me-back from-it except this the-news which I-heard about-you.
sentences.i: He said to her, “That is so; but God brought me back safe and sound, and I meant to travel again, and nothing kept me from it but this news I have heard of you.
sentences.n: ṣaḥīḥun, “true”, a one-word answer. bi-al-salāma, “in safety”: bi- “with”. radda, “to bring back”, and radda ʿan, “to turn back from”, the same verb twice in two senses; the shadda is printed on both ردّني. thāniyan, “a second time, again”. mā … illā, “nothing … but”.

sentences.t: فَاحْتَرَقَ قَلْبِي عَلَيْكِ وَجِئْتُ إِلَيْكِ لَعَلِّي أَنْ أُخَلِّصَكِ مِمَّا أَنْتِ فِيهِ
sentences.tr: fa-iḥtaraqa qalbī ʿalayki wa-jiʾtu ilayki laʿallī an ukhalliṣaki mimmā anti fīhi
sentences.l: So-burned my-heart over-you, and-I-came to-you; perhaps-I that I-free-you from-what you (are) in-it.
sentences.i: My heart burned for you, and I have come to you in the hope that I may free you from what you are in.”
sentences.n: iḥtaraqa ʿalā, Form VIII, “to burn (with grief) for”. laʿallī an ukhalliṣaki, “perhaps I may free you”: Classical laʿalla takes a plain imperfect, but here an is put before it, as after ʿasā; a Middle Arabic habit. The ئ of وجئت is printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ يَا أَخِي هَلْ أَنْتَ تَظُنُّ أَنَّ الَّذِي اعْتَرَانِي جُنُونٌ قَالَ نَعَمْ قَالَتْ لَا وَاللَّهِ وَإِنَّمَا هُوَ كَمَا قَالَ الشَّاعِرُ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu yā akhī hal anta taẓunnu anna alladhī iʿtarānī junūnun qāla naʿam qālat lā wa-Allāhi wa-innamā huwa kamā qāla al-shāʿiru
sentences.l: And-she-said to-him: O my-brother, (is it that) you think that what has-come-upon-me (is) madness? He-said: Yes. She-said: No, by-God, but-rather it (is) as said the-poet:
sentences.i: She said to him, “Brother, do you think that what has come over me is madness?” “Yes,” he said. She said, “No, by God; it is as the poet said:
sentences.n: hal, the question particle; anta is set before the verb for emphasis. iʿtarā, Form VIII, “to come upon, befall”, of an illness or a fit. wa-Allāhi, the wāw of oaths. innamā, “it is only, rather”. ka-mā, “as”: ka- “like”, with mā, “what”.

sentences.t:
قَالُوْا جُنِنْتَ بِمَنْ تَهْوَى فَقُلْتُ لَهُمْ * مَا لَذَّةُ الْعَيْشِ اِلَّا لِلْمَجَانِيْنِ
اَلْعِشْقُ لَايَسْتَفِيقُ الدَّهْرَ صَاحِبُهُ * وَاِنَّمَا يَصْرَعُ الْمَجْنُوْنَ فِي الْحِيْنِ
نَعَمْ جُنِنْتُ فَهَاتُوْا مَنْ جُنِنْتُ بِهِ * اِنْ كَانَ يَشْفِي جُنُونِي لَاتَلُوْمُوْنِي
sentences.tr:
qālū juninta bi-man tahwā fa-qultu lahum * mā ladhdhatu al-ʿayshi illā li-al-majānīni
al-ʿishqu lā yastafīqu al-dahra ṣāḥibuhu * wa-innamā yaṣraʿu al-majnūna fī al-ḥīni
naʿam junintu fa-hātū man junintu bihi * in kāna yashfī junūnī lā talūmūnī
sentences.l:
They-said: You-have-gone-mad with whom you-love. So-I-said to-them: * Not (is the) sweetness (of) the-life except for-the-madmen.
The-love: not recovers (in) the-time its-possessor, * whereas only fells the-madman in the-hour.
Yes, I-have-gone-mad; so-bring whom I-have-gone-mad with-him; * if is curing my-madness, do-not blame-me.
sentences.i:
They said, “You are mad for the one you love.” I answered them, * “The sweetness of life belongs to none but the mad.”
Love: the one who has it never comes to himself all his days, * whereas the madman is struck down only for a time.
Yes, I am mad; then bring me the one I am mad for, * and if he cures my madness, do not blame me.
sentences.n: The print points the verse, and its pointing is kept; it sets a sukūn on the long vowels of قَالُوْا, الْمَجْنُوْنَ and the like, writes the hamza of اِلَّا, اِنَّمَا, اِنْ as a vowel on bare alif, and puts a fatḥa on the alif of the article at the head of the second line, اَلْعِشْقُ, where it is pronounced. junintu, junintu: the passive of janna, “to be maddened”, literally “to be possessed by the jinn”; bi- marks the cause, “mad for”. In the first line juninta is “you”, in the third junintu is “I”. The second line sets love against madness: the lover never wakes (istafāqa, Form X, “to recover, come to oneself”), al-dahra, accusative of time, “for all time”; the madman is felled only fī al-ḥīn, “at a time”, in his fits. yaṣraʿu is active with the madman as object, the agent (the jinn, the fit) left unnamed. hātū, “bring!”, a defective imperative, plural. The plurals answer the “they said” of the first line. The print runs lā into its verbs, لَايَسْتَفِيقُ and لَاتَلُوْمُوْنِي; lā talūmūnī is the prohibition, the jussive talūmū with -nī, “me”. These lines are much quoted.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذٰلِكَ عَلِمَ مَرْزَوَانُ أَنَّهَا عَاشِقَةٌ فَقَالَ لَهَا احْكِي لِي عَلَى قِصَّتِكِ وَمَا أَصَابَكِ لَعَلَّ أَنْ يَكُونَ بِيَدِي شَيْءٌ أَفْعَلُهُ وَيَكُونُ فِيهِ خَلَاصُكِ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika ʿalima Marzawānu annahā ʿāshiqatun fa-qāla lahā iḥkī lī ʿalā qiṣṣatiki wa-mā aṣābaki laʿalla an yakūna bi-yadī shayʾun afʿaluhu wa-yakūnu fīhi khalāṣuki
sentences.l: So-at that, knew Marzawān that-she (was) in-love, and-he-said to-her: Tell me about your-story and-what has-befallen-you; perhaps that there-be in-my-hand something I-do-it, and-there-be in-it your-deliverance.
sentences.i: Then Marzawān knew that she was in love, and he said to her, “Tell me your story and what has befallen you; it may be that there is something in my power to do that will set you free.”
sentences.n: ʿāshiqa, “in love”, active participle of ʿashiqa. iḥkī, feminine imperative of ḥakā, “to tell”, regular as printed. ḥakā ʿalā, colloquial, “to tell about”, where Classical uses a direct object. laʿalla an yakūna, “perhaps it may be”: again an after laʿalla, the Middle Arabic habit met a few lines above. bi-yadī, “in my hand”, in my power: bi- “in”. afʿaluhu, “(which) I can do”, an imperfect standing as a relative clause after an indefinite noun. The tanwīn of شيءٌ is printed.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the-morning overtook Shahrazād, and-she-fell-silent from the-permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The closing formula, as at the end of every night.
